extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematical logic, set theory, and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly survey of Russell's paradox: its historical origin, various responses (typed and untyped), constructive and logical approaches, and the formal/logical principles that capture its pattern. Aimed at explaining and comparing methods for avoiding or reinterpreting the paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious-circle principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever involves all of a collection must not be one of the collection; if, provided a certain collection had a total, it would have members only definable in terms of that total, then the said collection has no total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a constraint on definitions of propositional functions: no propositional function may be defined prior to specifying exactly the objects in its domain. Used to motivate arranging propositional functions into a hierarchy (type theory) to block paradoxes arising from circularity. Example: before defining 'x is a prime number' one must have the domain N. Anti-pattern: permitting definitions that quantify over or presuppose the totality they are defining (illegitimate totalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutional (no-classes) theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A version of a no-classes theory (Russell 1906–1907) that attempts to avoid commitment to classes by treating class-talk substitutionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell's published description is sketchy; while it can yield a solution to Russell's paradox, it does not fully block diagonalization and faces its own paradoxes. It influenced Russell's later move to type theory. Aspiring scholars should study its motivations and limitations. Anti-pattern: assuming the substitutional account is a complete, paradox-free replacement for set/class ontologies without attending to diagonalization failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple and ramified type theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging sentences/propositional functions into a hierarchy (types) so that predicates/functions only apply to objects of appropriate lower types, avoiding self-reference and paradoxical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell's simple theory (1903) and ramified theory (1908/Principia) restrict formation of classes/functions to block the construction of R by diagonalization. Criticisms: seen by some as ad hoc; defenders (e.g., Andrews 1986) offer counterarguments. Note Russell later relaxed type restrictions for extensional mathematics (apply only to intensional entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's restriction limited to intensional entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's later view: type restrictions should be applied when characterizing intensional entities (e.g., propositional functions) but dropped for extensional mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mitigates the type-theoretic restrictions for mathematical practice while retaining them to block intensional paradoxes. Supported in later literature (Church 1978, Myhill 1979, Kripke 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's finitist/axiomatic demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a foundation for mathematics using only finite, well-defined, intuitively constructible objects and absolutely certain inference rules; give Cantorian set theory an axiomatic basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert hoped such definiteness would prevent paradoxes. This is a programmatic methodological constraint rather than a single axiom schema; it motivated axiomatizations of set theory. Anti-pattern: assuming informal intuition about infinite totalities suffices without axiomatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist requirement for construction procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not assert the existence of a mathematical object without providing a procedure for constructing it (Poincaré, Brouwer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré criticized Zermelo's separation for not requiring constructive procedures; Brouwer's intuitionism accepts existence only when supported by acceptable constructive procedures. This blocks illegitimate existence claims that could generate paradox. Anti-pattern: asserting existence via non-constructive intuition or unrestricted comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo's Axiom Schema of Separation (ZA)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A and formula φ (with B not free in φ), there exists B = {x in A : φ(x)}; i.e., comprehension is restricted to subcollections of an existing set A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ZA prevents forming problematic 'totalities' like V as a set; the argument shows V cannot be a set because separation relative to V would yield contradiction. Consequence: additional set-existence axioms become necessary to recover mathematics that full comprehension would have provided. Anti-pattern: applying unrestricted comprehension to the universe V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Von Neumann/Bernays–Gödel distinction sets vs. proper classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a member/non-member distinction: sets are objects that are elements of some class; proper classes (non-members) are not elements of any class. Only sets may be elements of classes, so paradoxical collections like R are proper classes, not sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This untyped strategy allows talking about large collections (proper classes) without making them members of classes (hence avoiding Russell's paradox). Modern versions are single-sorted class theories (Bernays–Gödel). Use this method to permit a universal-like V while avoiding treating V as a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quine's stratified comprehension / New Foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow a universal set V but require comprehension only for stratified formulas that prevent circularity; stratification imposes a hierarchy akin to types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks circularity differently from type theory; leads to interesting anomalies and has been critiqued relative to Zermelo-style theories (Martin 1970; Boolos 1971). Alternative untyped approaches exist that also allow a universal set (e.g., Church 1974b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ackermann-style class/set theory with predicate M
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat all objects as classes (upper-case variables) with extensionality, add a predicate M(x) to indicate which classes are sets, and restrict comprehension for sets so that the defining formula contains no occurrence of M and uses only set parameters (ACS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACS: if every class satisfying φ is a set (and φ contains no M and only set parameters), then there exists a set of exactly those classes. The restrictions on occurrences of M and parameters are essential; lifting them yields Russell's paradox. This approach is conservative (equivalent to ZF) but requires care to avoid illicit instantiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraconsistent approach (give up explosion/EFQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the impact of isolated contradictions by rejecting the classical principle that a contradiction entails every sentence (Ex Falso Quodlibet), thereby preventing trivialization from paradoxical instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding EFQ typically requires rejecting disjunctive syllogism or other classical inference principles; however, even abandoning EFQ is insufficient because Curry-like paradoxes (and the need to reject Contraction) can still lead to triviality. Radical changes to sentential logic and rules (e.g., modus ponens modifications) are required; such moves have costs and may not preserve the intended content of (NC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting Excluded Middle is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: One might try to avoid Russell's paradox by rejecting the law of excluded middle, but Russell's paradox can be formulated and derived using only intuitionistically acceptable methods (Law of Non-contradiction and modus tollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus intuitionism's rejection of excluded middle does not, by itself, avoid Russell's paradox. The paradox can be driven by non-EM reasoning, so more radical logical alterations are needed to block it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal lemma and its logical core (T269/TCL relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor's Diagonal Lemma (CL) — the diagonal set D_f = {x in X: x notin f(x)} cannot be in the range Y — is logically related to a pure first-order formula (T269) capturing Russell's pattern: ¬∃y ∀x (Fxy ≡ ¬Fxx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that Russell's paradox and Cantor's theorem share a close purely logical form: CL is a substitution/generalization instance of T269. This identifies a purely logical obstruction to certain totalities (no function onto the powerset). Use this to understand the generality of diagonal arguments across logic and set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of first-order reduction (Burali‑Forti example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all set-theoretic paradoxes reduce to first-order logical theorems; e.g., Burali‑Forti paradox involves well-orderings, which are not first-order definable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates the range of methods: some paradoxes are captured by first-order logical patterns (like T269) while others require higher-order or non-elementary resources to analyze, so method choice depends on the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological trade-offs among typed, untyped, constructivist, and logical-change strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Various strategies to handle Russell's paradox (type restrictions, limitation-of-size, separation schemas, class/set distinctions, stratification, constructivism, paraconsistency, plural quantification) each have costs and benefits regarding mathematical practice, expressive power, and philosophical plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey emphasizes comparing these approaches: typed theories restrict expressive freedom but block paradoxes; untyped class theories allow large collections but must distinguish sets/proper classes or restrict comprehension; constructivist approaches demand procedures but may limit classical reasoning; paraconsistent/logical-change approaches alter inference rules but face further paradoxes (e.g., Curry). Choice involves trade-offs for foundations and semantics; study current literature (e.g., Church, Quine, Ackermann, Boolos, Burgess, Kripke) to evaluate options.
